whyCorrect: The goal set by the stem is narrow: emphasize a difference between two specific works, Water Line and Seven Earth Mountain. That means the sentence has to name both works and put one detail about each side by side so they clash. The notes give you exactly the pair you need — Water Line is aluminum tubing, Seven Earth Mountain is soil — and this choice sets them against each other with "by contrast." Everything else in the notes (the memorial, the dates, the gallery-filling scale) is beside the point here.

whyWrong.A: It mentions only Water Line and pairs it with the Vietnam Veterans Memorial, so Seven Earth Mountain never appears — you cannot emphasize a difference between two works when one of them is missing.
whyWrong.B: It draws a similarity rather than a difference ("echoed in"), and it compares Water Line to the memorial instead of to Seven Earth Mountain.
whyWrong.D: It names both installations but groups them together as examples of one artist's output, which stresses what they have in common instead of what separates them.

commonMistakes: Choosing the option that uses the most notes. A rhetorical synthesis answer is judged only against the stated goal, so a sentence packed with accurate detail still fails if it does not do the one job the stem names.
tips: Underline the goal in the stem first, then check each choice against two things: does it mention every item the goal requires, and does the relationship it states (contrast, similarity, sequence) match the one asked for?

whyCorrect: The goal is to emphasize where the figures are placed in one painting, Lost in the Shuffle. Scan the notes for positional language and only one bullet supplies it: the two young men float in the bottom left and upper right corners of the canvas. This choice reproduces that placement and attaches it to the right painting, so the sentence does exactly the job the stem names.

whyWrong.A: It emphasizes the placid mood the paintings share, which is a different note entirely and says nothing about where any figure sits on the canvas.
whyWrong.C: It compares the canvas dimensions of the two paintings. Size is not location, and the choice is also garbled — the dimensions of Lost in the Shuffle have dropped out of "At by inches."
whyWrong.D: It emphasizes the colors Rawles uses for the water and covers both paintings at once, so it neither isolates Lost in the Shuffle nor mentions the figures' positions.

commonMistakes: Treating any sentence that mentions Lost in the Shuffle as on-target. Two of the wrong choices name the painting; what disqualifies them is that they emphasize mood, size, or color instead of position.
tips: Before reading the choices, find the one or two bullets that actually answer the goal — here, the only bullet containing corner-and-canvas language — and expect the correct choice to be built from those.

whyCorrect: The goal is to explain a concept, so the correct sentence has to work as a definition for a reader who has never met the term. Two bullets combine into one: an object heats up when twisted, and twisting is called torsion. Putting them together gives you torsional heating = temperature rising as a result of being twisted, which is precisely what this choice states. The fibers and the 2019 measurements are evidence about the concept, not the concept itself.

whyWrong.A: It says the temperature will "change," which drops the direction of the effect — heating specifically means an increase — and it uses the word "torsion" without explaining that torsion is twisting, so it defines nothing for a reader who does not already know the term.
whyWrong.C: It reports a comparison between two materials from the study's results. That is a finding produced by torsional heating, not an explanation of what torsional heating is.
whyWrong.D: It describes what the researchers did and which fibers they tested, using the term "torsional heating" as though it were already understood rather than explaining it.

commonMistakes: Picking the choice with the most study data. A goal of "explain the concept" is asking for a definition, and specific measurements are the one kind of detail a definition does not need.
tips: When the goal says explain or define, look for the choice that would still make sense to someone who never read the notes.

whyCorrect: The word "both" in the goal is doing the work: the sentence has to give the collection date of each of the two samples, not just one. The notes supply May 3, 1930 for Achyrocline vauthieriana and February 14, 1927 for Vernonia liatroides. This choice carries both dates and links them with "after," which keeps the emphasis on when rather than on where or on what family they belong to.

whyWrong.A: It emphasizes where the specimens can be viewed now, at the C.V. Starr Virtual Herbarium, and gives no collection date at all.
whyWrong.B: It dates only one sample, Achyrocline vauthieriana, so it fails the requirement that both dates appear; its date is also garbled, reading "On May in 1930" with the day dropped.
whyWrong.C: It gives both specimens but emphasizes the places they were found, Minas Gerais and Jalisco, along with their shared family — location and classification instead of time.

commonMistakes: Reading past "both" and accepting a choice that handles one sample correctly. When a goal names two items, a choice covering only one is wrong no matter how accurate it is.
tips: Check the goal for a quantity word — both, each, all — and count how many items the choice actually covers before judging anything else about it.
